title: Stacks and Queues
summary: Use last-in-first-out and first-in-first-out order to match nested structure and process items in arrival order.
lesson:
How it works
- A stack adds and removes at the top (LIFO); a queue adds at the back and removes at the front (FIFO).
- A deque supports both ends; in Java, `ArrayDeque` serves as a stack, a queue, or a deque with `O(1)` amortized operations.
- An array-backed stack doubles its capacity when full, so a push is `O(1)` amortized.

When to reach for it
- Input has nesting that must close in reverse order of opening, such as brackets or tags.
- You need the most recent unmatched item, or to undo the latest action.
- Items must be processed in the order they arrived, as in breadth-first search.
- You need the next greater or smaller element, or a running window maximum.

Common patterns
- Matching: push openers and pop on a closer, checking that they pair up.
- Monotonic stack or deque: pop elements that can never be the answer before pushing a new one.
- Queue-driven traversal: enqueue work as it is discovered and process it in order.

Pitfalls
- Popping or peeking an empty stack; check emptiness first, and check it again when input ends.
- Using `java.util.Stack`, which is synchronized and legacy; prefer `ArrayDeque`.
- Forgetting to clear references to removed elements in a hand-written array stack.
